bibliographic.title: Evidence-based AI: from trailblazer to trustblazer?
bibliographic.citation_apa: Luechtefeld, T., & Hartung, T. (2026). Evidence-based AI: from trailblazer to trustblazer? Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, 9, 1818128. https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2026.1818128

methodology.study_design: perspective article proposing Evidence-based Agent Stack
methodology.technology_context: agentic AI, large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, multi-step scientific workflows

eligibility.decision_rationale: Perspective peer-reviewed article on trustworthy agentic AI and LLM governance in high-stakes regulatory science and toxicology, with strong alignment to accountability, traceability, audit, and RAG. No evidence in the provided text addresses conversational AI, chatbots, or dialogue-system governance, so it is better classified as foundational/contextual rather than central conversational-governance evidence.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Python triage scored conversational_ai 0/3; manual confirmation needed that full text lacks conversational-system governance content and to verify framework details beyond provided excerpts.

appraisal.notes: Appropriate as a conceptual perspective proposing an operational framework; not an empirical study. Strong clarity on trust, provenance, and regulatory alignment, but no primary data collection or conversational-AI evaluation.

cerqual.explanation: Internally coherent framework for evidence-based agentic AI in regulated domains, but provided text is perspective-only, lacks conversational-AI focus, and offers limited direct evidence on conversational governance mechanisms.

coding.theme: Evidence-based governance framework for trustworthy agentic AI
coding.subtheme: Protocolized agent roles with mandatory provenance in regulatory and toxicology contexts

synthesis.main_claim: Agentic AI in high-stakes regulatory science and toxicology requires evidence-based workflows with traceability, reproducibility, provenance, and explicit uncertainty communication rather than fluent text generation alone.
synthesis.contribution: Proposes an Evidence-based Agent Stack that decomposes end-to-end tasks into protocolized roles with mandatory provenance and versioning, anchored in systematic review practice, risk-of-bias frameworks, and emerging regulatory principles.
synthesis.limitations: Perspective without primary empirical evaluation; provided excerpts emphasize incomplete reporting in LLM-assisted methods and risks of overfitting, prompt engineering masquerading as validation, and automation traps when evaluation does not scale with capability.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational/contextual evidence for governance of LLM-based agentic workflows in regulated domains, especially traceability, auditability, RAG grounding, and accountability; not as central evidence on conversational governance.

evidence.claim: Article is a peer-reviewed perspective in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence.
Focuses on agentic AI and LLMs in high-stakes regulated domains.
evidence.excerpt: Yet in high-stakes domains such as regulatory science and toxicology, fluent outputs are not sufficient

evidence.claim: Proposes Evidence-based Agent Stack with protocolized roles and provenance.
evidence.excerpt: We propose an Evidence-based Agent Stack that decomposes end-to-end tasks into protocolized roles

evidence.claim: Emphasizes accountability, auditable outputs, and decision alignment.
evidence.excerpt: systems whose outputs are auditable, updateable, and aligned with decision accountability

evidence.claim: Discusses LLM hallucinations and limits of fluency as truth proxy.
evidence.excerpt: Large language models are trained to produce likely continuations of text, not to guarantee factuality

evidence.claim: References governance instruments including NIST AI RMF and GenAI Profile.
evidence.excerpt: the NIST AI RMF frames trustworthiness as a lifecycle property

evidence.claim: Cites agentic AI with RAG examples in biomedicine and pharmacovigilance.
evidence.excerpt: TxAgent integrates multi-step reasoning with real-time knowledge grounding

evidence.claim: States LLM persuasive untestable narratives are operationally dangerous in hazard and policy decisions.
evidence.excerpt: an LLM that produces persuasive, untestable narratives is operationally dangerous

evidence.claim: Requires explicit labeling of inference and auditable chain of custody.
evidence.excerpt: inferred content must be labeled as inference rather than presented as extracted evidence

evidence.claim: Notes incomplete reporting in LLM-assisted evidence-synthesis methods.
evidence.excerpt: a tendency toward incomplete reporting in LLM papers (dataset splitting, prompt development, model choice, validation metrics)

evidence.claim: Warns that automation can degrade standards when evaluation lags capability.
evidence.excerpt: Automation can degrade scientific standards when evaluation and reporting do not keep pace with rapidly expanding capability

evidence.claim: No conversational AI, chatbot, or dialogue-system governance content in provided text.
